claim: The widely-circulated statistic that only 5-10% of creators reach sustainable full-time income traces, in at least one high-ranking vector, to an unbylined SEO content page that provides no sample, survey, year, platform, or citation for it.
stance_target: The 5-10% sustainable-income figure and the '90% of creators fail' framing built on it
scope_conditions: 'When Notes Fly', 9,219 words, no named author, no publication date; the page's own bibliography contains no source capable of producing this figure
quoted_support: The statistics are sobering: estimates suggest only 5-10% of creators who seriously attempt to build audiences reach sustainable full-time income levels. The remaining 90-95% either earn supplemental amounts, token revenue, or nothing at all.

claim: The claim that the median Patreon creator earns less than $150 annually is attributed only to 'research from platforms like Patreon' — a hedged non-attribution with no report, year, or sample behind it.
stance_target: The median Patreon creator earnings figure of <$150/year
scope_conditions: Undated; note that other sources in this corpus put the typical Patreon creator nearer $500/month per Graphtreon tracker data, an order-of-magnitude discrepancy that neither source reconciles
quoted_support: Research from platforms like Patreon shows that the median creator earns less than $150 annually, while the mean is pulled much higher by a tiny percentage of top earners.

claim: The claim that 96-97% of YouTube channels never reach the 1,000-subscriber and 4,000-watch-hour monetization threshold is stated with no data source, and is the origin point for the derived '4% of creators' framing that recurs across creator-economy commentary.
scope_conditions: Undated; YouTube; no cohort definition, no denominator (all channels ever created vs channels with any upload vs channels attempting monetization), which materially changes the number
quoted_support: On YouTube, data suggests 96-97% of channels fail to reach the 1,000 subscriber and 4,000 watch hour threshold required even to apply for monetization.

claim: A purported 2021 YouTube channel survival study by 'Rahul Nilakantan and Jaya Anindya' at IIM Calcutta, reported as tracking 50,000 channels over three years and finding 73% uploaded fewer than 10 videos before going inactive, could not be located in OpenAlex or in web search and appears to be fabricated.
stance_target: The evidentiary standing of any creator-survival figure sourced to this page
scope_conditions: Verification attempted July 2026 via OpenAlex full-text search, Semantic Scholar, and web search; no paper, preprint, working paper, or author pair matching this description was found at IIM Calcutta or elsewhere; the specificity of the figures (50,000 channels, six-month launch window, three-year tracking, 73%, a discontinuity at the 50th upload) is what makes the absence notable
quoted_support: Economists Rahul Nilakantan and Jaya Anindya at the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta published a 2021 analysis of YouTube channel survival rates using data from 50,000 channels launched in a single six-month period, tracking their performance over three years.
region: claimed India-based research on global YouTube data

claim: A purported 2022 Dweck and Haimovitz finding that fixed-mindset creators show 64% higher six-month attrition is not locatable in the psychological literature, and a web search for the claim returns the asserting page itself as the only source — a closed citation loop.
stance_target: Psychological explanations for creator attrition sourced to this page
scope_conditions: Verification attempted July 2026; Kyla Haimovitz and Carol Dweck are real collaborators but their joint published work concerns parents' failure mindsets (Psychological Science, 2016), not creator persistence; the search-result set for the specific claim contained only whennotesfly.com
quoted_support: Dweck and Haimovitz found that creators who interpreted initial low performance as evidence of fixed talent (fixed mindset) showed 64% higher attrition rates within the first six months than creators who interpreted the same low performance as feedback about strategy (growth mindset).

claim: A purported David Hesmondhalgh paper in New Media and Society (2021) on 'structured precarity', including a count of five YouTube monetization-threshold changes between 2014 and 2022, could not be located, though Hesmondhalgh is a genuine cultural-labour scholar at Leeds whose real work is adjacent to the topic.
stance_target: Structural-precarity explanations for creator attrition sourced to this page
scope_conditions: Verification attempted July 2026 via OpenAlex; the internal date range is also self-inconsistent — a 2021 paper cannot analyse threshold changes running to 2022
quoted_support: His analysis of YouTube's monetization threshold changes between 2014 and 2022 showed five significant changes, each of which reset the rules in ways that disproportionately affected mid-tier creators.

claim: A purported 2021 Substack internal-data disclosure that 22% of its creators with 1,000+ subscribers had previously run video or podcast content with limited success is not locatable in any Substack publication.
stance_target: Platform-migration and second-attempt-recovery claims sourced to this page
scope_conditions: Verification attempted July 2026; no such Substack data release found
quoted_support: Analysts at Substack published internal data in 2021 showing that approximately 22% of their creators with more than 1,000 subscribers had previously operated video or podcast content with limited success.

claim: The page's stated bibliography and its stated statistics are entirely disconnected: ten generic references (Wikipedia, a Pew teen social-media survey, Li Jin's HBR essay, Ericsson's 1993 deliberate-practice paper, Hagiu and Wright on multi-sided platforms) none of which could produce any figure asserted in the body.
stance_target: The appearance of scholarly grounding in long-form creator-economy commentary
scope_conditions: Full bibliography reviewed; three of the ten entries have no working link at all; none is a creator-income or creator-survival dataset
quoted_support: 1. 'Creator Economy,' Wikipedia... 9. Ericsson, K. Anders, et al. 'The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance,' Psychological Review, vol. 100, no. 3, 1993, pp. 363-406.

claim: The page asserts, without any source, that reaching $30,000-50,000 annually from content requires the top 2-5% of creators and $75,000+ requires the top 1% — precise percentile thresholds for living-wage attainment with no distribution behind them.
stance_target: Percentile thresholds for creator living-wage attainment
scope_conditions: Undated, no platform-specific dataset, no country; the accompanying view-count model (500,000-1,000,000 monthly views for $30,000-50,000) is also unsourced
quoted_support: Reaching $30,000-50,000 annually from creation, enough to potentially quit a day job in lower cost-of-living areas, requires reaching the approximate top 2-5% of creators across most platforms. Earning $75,000+ requires reaching the top 1%.

claim: The page concedes that creator quit rates cannot be measured from public data because platforms do not publish abandonment data, then proceeds to state quit-rate conclusions anyway — an explicit acknowledgement of the evidence gap immediately followed by unevidenced assertion.
stance_target: The finding that creator attrition rates are not publicly measurable
scope_conditions: Undated; the concession itself is the useful part and is independently corroborated by the absence of platform abandonment disclosures elsewhere in this corpus
quoted_support: The quit rate is difficult to measure precisely because platforms don't publish data on abandoned channels, but observable patterns are telling.
